case_name: Sumit Bansal v. MGI Developers and Promoters
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that where multiple cheques issued in connection with a single underlying transaction are dishonoured on different dates and followed by separate statutory notices, each dishonoured cheque gives rise to a distinct, independent cause of action under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - multiple complaints arising from the same transaction are not, by that fact alone, an abuse of process.
why_it_matters: Payees holding several post-dated or instalment cheques from the same debtor can pursue a separate Section 138 complaint for each dishonoured cheque without risking a challenge that the multiplicity of complaints is itself vexatious.

case_name: Kaveri Plastics v. Mahdoom Bawa Bahrudeen Noorul
holding_summary: The Supreme Court quashed a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act complaint where the statutory demand notice sought Rs. 2 crore although the dishonoured cheque was for Rs. 1 crore, holding that a demand notice must claim the exact cheque amount and that even this kind of discrepancy is fatal to the complaint's maintainability.
why_it_matters: Drafting a Section 138 demand notice for anything other than the precise cheque amount, including by inadvertent error, can be fatal to the resulting criminal complaint, making careful notice drafting essential before initiating cheque-bounce proceedings.

case_name: Arenel Private Limited v. M/s. Aakash Packaging
holding_summary: A Division Bench of the Bombay High Court held that an arbitral award that relies on irrelevant material or ignores relevant evidence on record violates fundamental principles of justice and can be set aside under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, upholding a Single Judge's decision that had set aside part of a December 2019 award in a packaging-materials supply dispute for reliance on hearsay over the parties' own laboratory reports.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that Indian courts will look past an arbitrator's findings of fact where the award is shown to rest on irrelevant material or to have disregarded directly relevant documentary evidence such as contemporaneous lab reports - a useful precedent for parties challenging awards on the patent-illegality/fundamental-justice ground.

case_name: The Reporters Collective Trust & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M. Pancholi, issued notice on petitions challenging Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 - which amended Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act to create a blanket exemption for personal information - along with a related challenge to Section 36 of the DPDP Act and Rule 23 of the DPDP Rules empowering government to call for information from data fiduciaries. The Court referred the core constitutional questions to a larger Bench while declining to stay operation of the DPDP framework in the meantime.
why_it_matters: Public authorities, RTI applicants and data fiduciaries should treat the DPDP Act's blanket RTI exemption for personal information as fully operative for now, since the Supreme Court declined any interim stay, while a larger Bench reference on its constitutionality remains pending.

case_name: In Re: Functioning of State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions in Low-Pendency States (Suo Motu)
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 11 February 2026
holding_summary: A Bench led by the Chief Justice, with Justice Joymalya Bagchi, invoked Article 142 of the Constitution to direct that sitting High Court judges in States and Union Territories that have found it not viable to constitute full-fledged State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions - including Sikkim, Manipur, Goa, Mizoram, Nagaland, Himachal Pradesh, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Meghalaya - will hear pending consumer complaints and appeals, functioning as deemed Chairpersons of the State Commission for that purpose.
why_it_matters: Consumers and businesses with pending consumer appeals in low-pendency States and UTs that lack a functioning State Commission now have a clear route to have those matters heard by a designated High Court judge instead of waiting indefinitely for a commission to be constituted.

case_name: The Managing Director, KSRTC v. P. Chandramouli & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pankaj Mithal and Prasanna B. Varale held that amounts received by the dependants of a deceased accident victim under an employer-provided group insurance scheme or other independent contractual/social-security benefit cannot be deducted from the compensation awarded under the Motor Vehicles Act, since such benefits arise from a separate contractual relationship with no requisite nexus to statutory motor accident compensation.
why_it_matters: Claimants receiving employer-linked group insurance or similar benefits after a fatal motor accident can be assured those amounts will not be set off against their MACT compensation, preserving the full value of both entitlements.

holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar held that an application under Section 29A(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to extend an arbitral tribunal's mandate is maintainable even after expiry of the statutory time limit under Sections 29A(1) and (3), and even where an award has already been rendered during the interim period. The Court noted that an award passed after the mandate has expired is unenforceable and non est, but that an arbitrator's error in passing such an award does not deprive the court of jurisdiction to entertain a later extension application.
why_it_matters: Parties whose arbitral tribunal issues an award after its Section 29A mandate has technically lapsed are not left without a remedy - they can still apply to extend the mandate after the fact, rather than being forced to restart arbitration from scratch.

case_name: Hindustan Unilever Limited v. Kwick Living (I) Private Limited
holding_summary: In HUL's disparagement and trademark suit over Kwick Living's comparative advertising campaign against Vim and Surf Excel, a Division Bench (Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani) held that principles of territorial jurisdiction are not diluted merely because allegedly infringing content is accessible over the internet across India. While deciding jurisdiction for the dispute before it, the Bench referred to a Larger Bench the broader questions of how Section 20 CPC, Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act, and Section 62 of the Copyright Act interact to fix jurisdiction for suits arising from online advertising and e-commerce sales.
why_it_matters: Until the Larger Bench rules, companies bringing or defending IP and comparative-advertising suits over online content can no longer assume they may sue wherever their goods or ads are digitally accessible; where the corporate plaintiff's registered office sits will remain a live jurisdictional question.

case_name: Kavitha Kuruganti v. PepsiCo India Holdings Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran declined to revoke PepsiCo India's registration of its FL 2027 (FC-5) potato variety, used for Lay's chips, under Section 34(h) of the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, holding that having earlier sued (and then withdrawn suits against) Gujarat farmers for infringement did not itself justify revocation. The Court simultaneously held that individual farmers sued for using protected seed can invoke the statutory farmers' privilege under Section 39(1)(iv) of the PPVFR Act to save, use, sow, exchange or sell farm produce, including seed of a protected variety.
why_it_matters: Reportedly the first Supreme Court ruling construing the PPVFR Act's registration and farmers'-rights provisions together, giving seed/agri companies clarity that pursuing (even later-withdrawn) infringement suits will not itself void a variety's registration, while confirming farmers retain a statutory shield against such suits.

case_name: M/s Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation v. Central Board of Trustees & Anr.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, while resolving appeals over provident fund and gratuity dues owed to workmen in an insolvency-resolution context, referred to a larger Bench the question whether the authorised officer has discretion under Section 14B of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 to levy less than full damages for default, or whether imposition of maximum damages is mandatory. The Court directed EPF dues, together with Section 7Q interest, be paid in four quarterly instalments from December 2026.
why_it_matters: Employers facing EPF default penalties - including those emerging from insolvency resolution plans - now face an unsettled but live question on whether authorities must impose maximum Section 14B damages or retain discretion to moderate them, pending the larger Bench's ruling.

case_name: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II v. Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu restored an NCLAT appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC that had been dismissed as time-barred, after the appellant's counsel made a bona fide attempt to e-file on the last day of limitation but could not because of a backend technical glitch in NCLAT's own e-filing portal, with the appeal actually filed only one day late. Invoking the principle that an act of the court should prejudice no one, the Court held the period during which the portal was non-functional could be excluded, and remitted the matter to NCLAT to decide afresh whether sufficient cause existed to condone any residual delay.
why_it_matters: Litigants who can show a genuine, timely attempt to e-file before an IBC appeal deadline now have Supreme Court authority to seek exclusion of time lost to a tribunal's own portal failure, rather than being shut out by NCLAT's otherwise strict 45-day limitation regime.

case_name: Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. & Piccadily Hotels Pvt. Ltd. v. Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
citation: Appeal, Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (judgment dated 17 September 2026)
holding_summary: A Bench of Judicial Member Virender Bhat and Technical Member Ajay Talegaonkar dismissed the appeal of Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. and group company Piccadily Hotels Pvt. Ltd., upholding HERC's denial of 'captive user' status for power banked from Piccadily Agro's 17 MW biomass co-generation plant to the hotel unit, since Piccadily Hotels held only 14.57% equity in the generating company against the 26% minimum ownership threshold prescribed under the Electricity Rules, 2005. The Tribunal directed payment of outstanding banking-benefit dues of over Rs. 68 lakh to the discom.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that intra-group captive-power arrangements must strictly satisfy the 26% equity and 51% self-consumption thresholds under the Electricity Rules, or risk losing captive status - and associated open-access/cross-subsidy benefits - regardless of a power-banking agreement between group companies.

case_name: Koenig Solutions Pvt. Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner, Audit Branch
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court quashed a special-audit communication issued in Form GST ADT-03 and a consequential DRC-01 against Koenig Solutions for FY 2018-19, after the GST department conceded that no final order under Section 73 of the CGST Act had been passed by the statutory deadline of 30 April 2024. The Court held the audit process could not be kept alive indefinitely once the time limit for the underlying demand order had lapsed.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers facing open-ended GST special audits or notices tied to a financial year whose Section 73 limitation has already expired can rely on this ruling to have stale audit communications and demand notices quashed outright.

case_name: National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Co-location & Dark Fibre Settlement)
citation: Civil appeals arising from SAT order (disposed 18 September 2026)
holding_summary: The Supreme Court permitted a settlement between NSE and SEBI in the decade-old algorithmic-trading co-location and dark-fibre cases, under which NSE will pay approximately Rs. 1,491.21 crore under SEBI's settlement mechanism (Rs. 1,223.56 crore for co-location and Rs. 267.65 crore for the dark-fibre matter), disposing of SEBI's pending appeals against the Securities Appellate Tribunal's 2023 order that had earlier set aside SEBI's disgorgement direction.
why_it_matters: Brings finality to one of India's longest-running securities-market enforcement disputes and signals the Supreme Court's willingness to permit large-scale regulatory settlements even after years of SAT and appellate litigation - a template other market infrastructure institutions facing SEBI proceedings may look to.

case_name: Sai Consulting Engineers Pvt. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India & Ors.
citation: Delhi High Court, judgment dated 11 August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Sachin Datta quashed NHAI's two-year debarment of consultancy firm Sai Consulting Engineers from future bids - imposed over alleged breaches of a 2018 consultancy agreement for Detailed Project Reports on several bypass/ring-road projects - holding that an ordinary contractual breach unaccompanied by fraud or collusion cannot justify blacklisting. The debarment order was set aside while NHAI's right to separately claim damages for the alleged breach was expressly preserved.
why_it_matters: Reinforces the high threshold - fraud, collusion or moral turpitude, not mere contractual default - that government authorities like NHAI must meet before blacklisting a contractor or consultant, an important check for infrastructure-sector service providers facing debarment action.

case_name: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Trupti Sanjay Mehta & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva held that a bank can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to recover a secured loan it acquired by assignment from an NBFC, even though that NBFC was not a 'financial institution' covered by the Act at the time the loan was originally created, setting aside a Bombay High Court ruling that had restricted Kotak Mahindra Bank from enforcing SARFAESI against a loan portfolio it had acquired from City Financial Consumer Finance Ltd.
why_it_matters: Confirms that banks and ARCs acquiring loan books from non-SARFAESI-covered NBFCs and other lenders can still use SARFAESI's summary enforcement mechanism, removing significant legal uncertainty from the secondary loan-sale and securitisation market.

case_name: Nikhil Mehta & Anr. v. Gardenview Abode Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of President Justice A.P. Sahi and Member Bharatkumar Pandya declined to entertain a consumer complaint against the developer of Bengaluru's 'Mantri Blossom' project (formerly Mantri Developers, now Gardenview Abode) seeking a refund the complainants had already secured with interest from the Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority for the same booking, applying the doctrine of election to bar parallel proceedings for the same relief, while leaving the complainants free to enforce the existing K-RERA order.
why_it_matters: Confirms that homebuyers who have already obtained an enforceable refund order from RERA cannot separately pursue an overlapping consumer complaint for the same relief, underscoring the need to choose one forum - RERA or the consumer commission - and see it through.

case_name: Havells India Limited & Anr. v. Havai Home Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: Justice Jyoti Singh held that a defendant's own trademark registration for 'HAVAI' is no defence to a passing-off action where the plaintiff shows prior goodwill in 'HAVELLS', deceptive similarity and likelihood of consumer confusion, and restrained Havai Home Products from using the 'HAVAI' word and device marks, or any other mark deceptively similar to the Havells marks, assessing passing off by reference to actual stylisation, colour scheme and market presentation rather than merely the registered form of the mark.
why_it_matters: Reaffirms for brand owners that obtaining a trademark registration for a deceptively similar mark does not immunise a junior user from a passing-off injunction, keeping the legal focus on actual marketplace conduct and consumer confusion rather than registry status.
